slides.title: Memory Management & Hierarchy
slides.body: Memory Management & Hierarchy
slides.notes: Now we will be learning about the Memory Management & Hierarchy

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body: Introduction
slides.notes: Imagine your study table. It has limited space, so you can only keep the books you're currently using, while the rest stay on the shelf. Similarly, a computer also has limited main memory, and the operating system decides which programs should stay in memory and which should wait. This process is known as Memory Management.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Memory holds data and instructions while a program is running
CPU takes everything it needs from memory during execution
What is Memory?
slides.notes: Before we understand Memory Management, let's first understand what memory actually is. Whenever you open an application, whether it's a browser, a music player, or a document editor, the operating system loads its instructions and data into main memory. This is because the CPU cannot execute a program directly from storage. Instead, it fetches everything it needs from memory during execution. In simple terms, memory acts as the CPU's working area, providing quick access to the data and instructions required to run a program.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Tracks memory usage  which parts are free and which are allocated
Allows programs larger than RAM to run by moving data between RAM and storage
Gives programs a view of large memory even if physical memory is small
Protects memory so one process cannot corrupt another
Enables sharing of memory so multiple programs can efficiently use available space
Why is it required?
slides.notes:
Now, let's understand why memory management is important. It keeps track of 
which memory is currently in use and which part is free. It also allows large programs to 
run by moving data between RAM and storage when needed. At the same time,
 it gives programs the impression of having more memory than what's physically available,
 protects one process from accessing another's memory, and helps multiple programs use the available memory efficiently.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
What is Memory Hierarchy?
Memory Hierarchy is a structure that arranges memory into different levels based on
Closer to CPU → Faster but expensive
1
2
Farther from CPU → Slower but cheaper & bigger
slides.notes: Moving on, let's understand the concept of memory hierarchy. It organizes different types of memory based on factors like speed, cost, size, and how close they are to the CPU. In general, memory that is closer to the CPU is faster but more expensive and has lower capacity. On the other hand, memory farther from the CPU is slower, but it is cheaper and can store much more data.

1. Primary Memory
slides.notes:
Next, let's start with the first level of the memory hierarchy, which is primary memory. 
This is the memory used while programs are actively running, so the CPU can access 
data quickly. Since speed is the priority, it is faster but has limited storage capacity, and the data is stored only temporarily.

One important thing to remember is that this memory is volatile, meaning all the stored data is lost when the power is turned off.

slides.title: Memory Management Requirements
slides.body: Memory Management Requirements
slides.notes: Now we will learn about the Memory Management Requirements

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Main Requirements
Programs may be moved in memory during execution, addresses must adjust automatically
Relocation
Each process must be prevented from accessing others’ memory without permission
Protection
slides.notes:
Now, let's look at two important requirements of memory management. Relocation means a program can be moved to a different memory location during execution, 
and its addresses are updated automatically. Protection ensures that each process can access only its own memory, preventing unauthorized access to another process's data.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Main Requirements
Multiple processes should be able to share common code or data safely and efficiently
Sharing
Programs are written in logical modules, while memory is physically linear, OS maps logical structure to physical memory
Logical & Physical Organization
slides.notes: Moving on, let's look at two more requirements of memory management. Sharing allows multiple processes to safely use the same code or data without affecting each other. Logical and physical organization means that while programs are written in logical modules, the operating system maps them to the actual physical memory for efficient execution.

slides.title: Memory Management Unit
slides.body: Memory Management Unit
slides.notes: Next we will look into Memory Management Unit

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
How Translation Happens?
U
M
Memory
Management 
Unit
The Memory Management Unit (MMU) is a hardware component that manages how the CPU accesses memory, its main job is to convert the logical (virtual) addresses used by programs into physical addresses in RAM
slides.notes: Next, whenever a program runs, it works with logical or virtual addresses, not the actual locations in RAM. The responsibility of the MMU, which is a hardware component, is to convert these logical addresses into the corresponding physical addresses, so the CPU can access the required data from memory.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
How Translation Happens?
Uses a relocation register to convert each logical address into its physical address
Translation is automatic and hidden from programs
Allows programs to run without knowing real memory positions
 Memory is accessed using logical (virtual) addresses and physical addresses
slides.notes: Moving on, once a program generates a logical address, the system uses a relocation register to automatically convert it into the corresponding physical address. This entire translation happens in the background, so the program doesn't need to know where it is actually stored in memory. That's why memory access is based on logical and physical addresses.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Logical Address 
A logical address is the address generated by the CPU while a program is running, it is the virtual address that the program uses, and it does not exist physically in RAM
CPU
Program
Logical address
slides.notes: Next, let's understand what a logical address is. Whenever a program is executed, the CPU generates a logical address to access memory. This is the address that the program works with, but it doesn't represent the actual location in RAM. The actual physical location is determined later through address translation.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Logical Address 
Logical Address space
The logical address space is the range of all addresses a program can generate
Programs always work with logical addresses
MMU converts them to physical addresses before accessing memory
slides.notes: Now, instead of a single logical address, a program can generate many addresses during its execution. The complete range of these addresses is called the logical address space. Since programs always work with logical addresses, the MMU converts each one into a physical address before the memory is accessed.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Logical Address Space
Example
If a program's logical addresses run from:
0
4999

5000
Generated by the CPU
Used only by the program itself 
Never touches RAM directly
Every process gets its own logical address space, always starting from 0 (or a fixed base), regardless of where it will actually sit in RAM
slides.notes: Let's understand this with an example. Suppose a program has logical addresses ranging from 0 to 4999. This means the program has a logical address space of 5000 addresses. These addresses are generated by the CPU and are used only by the program during execution. They do not refer to the actual locations in RAM. Instead, the operating system later translates these logical addresses into physical addresses before accessing memory.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Physical Address
A physical address is the actual location in RAM where data is stored
The physical address space contains all real memory locations in RAM
slides.notes: Next, let's look at the physical address. Unlike a logical address, this is the actual location in RAM where the data is stored. The complete set of these real memory locations is known as the physical address space, and this is what the system ultimately uses to access memory.

slides.title: Physical Address Space
slides.body:
Actual Memory Address Range
The complete set of physical addresses that actually exist in RAM
Example
This is one shared space, unlike logical address space
All running processes' physical addresses live within this single range
The MMU maps each process's logical address space into some portion of this shared physical address space
For 4GB of RAM, physical address space = 0 to ~4,294,967,295 (4GB)
slides.notes: Moving on, the physical address space refers to the complete range of actual memory addresses available in RAM. For example, if a system has 4 GB of RAM, the physical addresses range from 0 to around 4.29 billion. Unlike logical address spaces, which are separate for each process, there is only one shared physical address space. The MMU maps each process's logical addresses to a suitable location within this shared memory.

slides.title: Memory Management Unit
slides.body:
Relocation Register
CPU register that holds the base (smallest) physical address of a process
How it works?
Physical address = Logical address + Relocation register value
Translation done at runtime by the MMU
slides.notes: Now, let's understand the role of the relocation register. It stores the starting, or base, physical address of a process in memory. Whenever the CPU generates a logical address, the MMU adds the relocation register value to it, giving the corresponding physical address. This translation happens automatically while the program is running.

slides.title: Memory Management Unit
slides.body:
Relocation Register
Example
Relocation reg = 14000, logical addr = 346 
Physical addr = 14346
Allows a program to be loaded anywhere in memory (dynamic relocation)
Works with limit register for memory protection
slides.notes: Moving on, let's see how the relocation register works with an example. If the relocation register stores 14,000 and the program generates a logical address of 346, the MMU combines them to get the physical address 14,346. This allows the same program to be loaded anywhere in memory without changing its code. Along with the limit register, it also helps ensure the process accesses only its allocated memory.

The MMU uses the Relocation Register to translate this logical address into a physical address by adding the relocation value. In this example, the logical address 346 is combined with the relocation value 14000, resulting in the physical address 14346. This translated address is then used to access the required location in main memory.

slides.title: Address Binding
slides.body: Address Binding
slides.notes: Next let’s learn about the Address Binding

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Address Binding
The process of mapping logical addresses → physical addresses
What is Address Binding?
Logical Addresses
Physical Addresses
Mapping
Address Binding is required because programs don’t know their final location in memory
slides.notes: Next, let's understand address binding. It is the process of connecting the logical addresses used by a program to the corresponding physical addresses in memory. This mapping is necessary because, while a program is being created, it doesn't know where it will finally be loaded in RAM.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Address Binding
Programs may be loaded at different memory locations
OS may move processes during execution
Ensures correct address translation at every stage
Supports relocation, protection, and virtual memory
What is Address Binding?
slides.notes: Moving on, address binding makes sure a program can run correctly even if it is loaded at different memory locations or moved by the operating system during execution. It ensures that address translation remains accurate at every stage and also supports important features like relocation, memory protection, and virtual memory.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Types of Address Binding
Address Binding
Execution-Time (Run-Time Binding)

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Types of Address Binding
Memory location known during compilation
Compiler generates absolute addresses
Program must be recompiled if loaded elsewhere
1. Compile-Time Binding
slides.notes: Now, suppose the operating system already knows where a program will be placed in memory before it is compiled. In that case, the compiler directly generates absolute memory addresses for that location. Since these addresses are fixed, if the program needs to be loaded somewhere else later, it has to be recompiled.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Types of Address Binding
2. Load-Time Binding
Exact location known only when program is loaded
Loader adjusts addresses → produces relocatable code
slides.notes: Moving on, in load-time binding, the program's memory location isn't decided during compilation. Instead, the loader determines the actual location when the program is loaded into memory and updates the addresses accordingly. This produces relocatable code, allowing the program to be loaded at different memory locations without recompiling.

slides.title: Memory Management
slides.body:
Types of Address Binding
3. Execution-Time (Run-Time) Binding
Final binding happens while program executes
Program can move during execution (swapping, compaction)
Requires MMU for dynamic address translation
slides.notes: Next, in execution-time binding, the actual memory address is decided while the program is running. This allows the operating system to move the program during execution, such as during swapping or compaction, without interrupting it. To support this dynamic address translation, the system relies on the MMU

slides.title: Address Binding — Compare at a Glance
slides.body: When Does Each Type Happen?

slides.title: Address Binding
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Think of booking a hotel room. You can be assigned a room number when you book (in advance), when you check in (at arrival), or be moved to a different room during your stay (while you're already there). Similarly, a program's logical address can be bound to a physical memory address at compile-time, load-time, or run-time —and when this binding happens determines whether the program can be moved later or not

slides.title: Swapping, Loader & Linker
slides.body: Swapping, Loader & Linker
slides.notes: Next we will learn about the Swapping, Loader & Linker

slides.title: Loader & Linker — Introduction
slides.body:
Getting a Program Ready to Run
Linker
Combines your compiled code with other object files and libraries into a single executable file
After a program is compiled, it isn't ready to run yet — two more steps happen first
Loader
Takes that executable and brings it into RAM so the CPU can actually run it
slides.notes: Now, once compilation is complete, the program still can't be executed immediately because a few preparation steps are required. First, the linker brings together the compiled program and any required libraries or object files to create a single executable. Once that's ready, the loader places that executable into RAM, making it available for the CPU to start execution.

slides.title: Getting a Program Ready to Run
slides.body:
Order
Both can work in two ways — static (done fully in advance) or dynamic (done partly at runtime) — covered next
Compile
Link
Load
Execute
slides.notes: Moving on, these are the four stages a program goes through before it starts running. It is first compiled, then linked to create an executable, loaded into memory, and finally executed by the CPU. Also, the linking and loading steps can happen either statically, where everything is prepared in advance, or dynamically, where part of the work is done while the program is running.

slides.title: Loader
slides.body:
What is Loader ?
Loading is done by a loader to bring programs into RAM
Loader
Load Programs
RAM
slides.notes: Now, once the executable file is ready, it still resides on secondary storage, so the CPU cannot execute it directly. The job of the loader is to transfer that program into RAM, because programs must be present in main memory before execution can begin. In simple terms, the loader acts as the bridge between the executable file and the memory where it actually runs.

slides.title: Loader
slides.body:
Static vs Dynamic Loading
Static Loading
Dynamic Loading
Entire program is loaded into memory at once
Uses more memory
Only loads parts of the program when needed
Saves memory, unused parts stay on disk until required
Loading
slides.notes: Next, there are two ways a program can be loaded into memory. In static loading, the entire program is placed into RAM before execution begins, which is simple but occupies more memory even if some parts are never used. In dynamic loading, only the required parts are loaded when the program actually needs them, so unused portions remain on the disk, helping save memory.

slides.title: Static vs Dynamic Loading
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A loader is like bringing a book from the shelf and placing it on your table before reading. It loads the program from storage into memory so it can run.

slides.title: Linker
slides.body:
What is Linker
Linking combines object files and libraries to create an executable
Object Files
libraries
slides.notes: Now, when a program is compiled, it is often split into multiple object files, and it may also depend on pre-written libraries for common functions. The linker brings all these pieces together, resolves their connections, and creates a single executable file that is ready to be loaded into memory for execution.

slides.title: Linker
slides.body:
Static vs Dynamic Linking
Static Linking
All libraries are added inside the executable
No need for external files during execution
Larger file size, but no runtime dependency
slides.notes: Moving on, in static linking, all the required library code is copied directly into the executable while it is being created. As a result, the program doesn't have to look for those libraries when it runs, making it independent of external library files. The trade-off, however, is that the executable becomes larger because it already contains all the required library code.

slides.title: Linker
slides.body:
Static vs Dynamic Linking
Dynamic Linking
Some libraries are loaded at runtime
Uses small stub to load functions when needed
Saves space and easier updates
slides.notes: Next, in dynamic linking, the executable doesn't contain the complete library code. Instead, it includes a small stub that knows how to locate and load the required library functions at runtime. This keeps the executable smaller and also makes updating shared libraries easier, since the program can use the latest library version without being rebuilt.

slides.title: Static vs Dynamic Linking
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A linker is like combining different chapters, notes, and references into one complete book. It combines program parts and libraries to create a single executable file.

slides.body:

Swapping is the process of moving a process's memory contents between RAM and a reserved area on secondary storage called swap space.
Swapping
slides.notes: Now, sometimes the operating system runs out of free RAM while multiple processes need to execute. In that situation, it can swap out a process by temporarily moving its memory contents from RAM to a reserved area on secondary storage called swap space, creating room for other processes. When that process needs to run again, it is swapped back into RAM, allowing execution to continue from where it left off.

slides.notes: Next, let's understand what swap in and swap out actually mean. Swap out happens when the operating system moves a process from RAM to swap space to free up memory for other processes. Later, when that process is needed again, swap in moves it back from swap space to RAM, so it can continue executing from where it was paused.

slides.title: Swapping
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Think of a study table with limited space. You keep only the books you are currently using on the table and move unused books back to the shelf. Similarly, OS moves inactive processes to disk and brings them back when needed.
